title: A hundred moons
hook: if a hundred moons rose and a thousand suns, without the Guru it would still be dark (Asa di Var M2, ang 463)

segments.voice: Yesterday, balihaaree, and your line: made angels of men. Did a late thank-you go out? A week ends today: peace in remembering, Sukhmani whole, Sukhmani kept; then var, the dawn ballad, its borrowed tune, and its first thanks. Now, the second Guru speaks. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

A stadium at night, every floodlight on. Every seat, every sign, every blade of grass lit up. And in the middle of all that light, someone sits who still doesn't know where they're going, or why. They can read every word on the scoreboard, and none of it tells them which way to turn. A life can look like that: full of light, information, options, screens, and inside, somehow still dark. Guru Angad has a salok for exactly that.
screen: `A STADIUM, EVERY LIGHT ON.` → `SOMEONE IN THE MIDDLE, STILL LOST.` → `A HUNDRED MOONS.`

segments.voice: Right after Guru Nanak's opening salok of thanks comes a second salok, by Guru Angad, the second Guru. In paraphrase: if a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns came up, even with all that light, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness. Chand is moon. Sooraj is sun. Chaanan is light, the ordinary Punjabi word for brightness, daylight, a lamp's glow. And ghor andhaar is deep, pitch-black darkness. Notice the size of the picture. One moon is enough to walk home by. One sun is enough for a whole world. Guru Angad multiplies them, a hundred and a thousand, as if to say: pile up all the outer light you like. It doesn't reach the place he means. That place is inside. The light that tells you who you are, what matters, which way to turn. In Sikh teaching that light comes through the Guru: the Word that teaches from within, carried by the Gurus and now by the Guru Granth Sahib. Without it, a person can be surrounded by brightness and still be stumbling. Set it beside yesterday's salok. Guru Nanak gave thanks for a Guru who turns humans into angels. Guru Angad explains why the thanks runs so deep: everything else, however bright, still leaves us in the dark. This is the voice of a student, too. Guru Angad was Guru Nanak's disciple before he became Guru. Here, in his own salok, he says what his teacher meant to him.
screen: `GURU ANGAD'S SALOK.` · `A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.` · `GHOR ANDHAAR: STILL PITCH DARK.` · `THE LIGHT THAT IS INSIDE.` · then, large: `THE GURU IS THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in the dark a moment. If you can, turn off the lights or close the curtains, or simply close your eyes and cup your hands over them. Let the darkness be complete. Sit in it without hurrying. Notice that even here, something in you is awake: the breath, the knowing that you're here. Rest in that inner light, quiet and small. If you pray, you can say Waheguru into the dark. The bell holds the time.
Chaanan, light or brightness: Guru Angad's salok asks what a hundred moons and a thousand suns, all that chaanan, can do, leaving pitch darkness without the Guru, the light within.
Your line: the guru is the light. Tonight, before you turn off the last light, sit for a breath in the dark and notice what's still lit inside. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Asa di Var's second salok, by Guru Angad, is sung each morning in gurdwaras: a hundred moons and a thousand suns would still leave darkness without the Guru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chaanan, light or brightness; the salok asks what all that chaanan can do without the Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hundred moons is a picture of a bright night.
what it means: no amount of outer light can reach the inner dark; that light comes through the Guru.
what a scholar hears: the salok is Mahala 2, by Guru Angad, set right after Guru Nanak's opening salok, so student and teacher speak back to back.

notes: Paraphrase of Guru Angad's salok (je sau chandaa ugvahi sooraj charhahi hajaar; ete chaanan hodiaa gur bin ghor andhaar): confirm.
